results.title: Organic vs Paid Social Media: How to Use Both (2026)
results.markdown:
Title: Organic vs Paid Social Media: How to Use Both (2026)

URL Source: https://turrboo.com/blog/organic-vs-paid-social-media

Markdown Content:
Each approach does a different job. Organic shows you which content your audience values. Paid takes that content to more people, faster, with precise targeting.

Both sit at the center of [social media marketing](https://turrboo.com/blog/what-is-social-media-marketing), and investment in paid keeps climbing. WARC forecasts global social media ad spend will grow 21.3% to $394.6bn in 2026, the strongest growth of any channel it tracks ([WARC, October 2026](https://www.warc.com/article/global-ad-spend-outlook-q-3-2026-eb1a9505c8d34d1fb3833cf61f675165)).

This guide covers how each approach works, what to measure, when to prioritize each, and how to run both from a single plan.

Organic social media is content you publish to your profiles without paying for distribution: posts, Reels, Stories, and replies. Paid social media is content you pay a platform to show to a chosen audience, such as boosted posts and ads. Organic builds trust over time. Paid buys immediate, measurable reach.

The two approaches differ most on speed, control, and what happens when you stop investing.

| Factor | Organic social media | Paid social media |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cost | No ad spend; costs staff time | Ad budget plus staff time |
| Speed to results | Slow, compounds over months | Fast, often within days |
| Reach | A share of your followers, set by the algorithm | Scales with budget and targeting |
| Audience control | Low | High: location, age, interests, behavior, retargeting |
| Trust | Higher; reads as the brand's own voice | Lower; carries a sponsored label |
| When you stop | Past posts keep working | Reach ends when the budget ends |
| Core metrics | Reach, engagement rate, saves, shares, follower growth | CTR, CPC, CPM, cost per result, ROAS |
| Best for | Community, trust, testing ideas | Launches, lead generation, reaching cold audiences |

Neither column wins outright. Each one covers the other's weak spot, which is why most brands run both.

*   Feed posts, carousels, short videos, and Stories published to your own profiles (the [types of social media posts](https://turrboo.com/blog/types-of-social-media-posts) most brands rotate)
*   Replies to comments, DMs, and reviews
*   Employees sharing company posts on their own profiles
*   Reposting customer content with permission
*   [Google Business Profile](https://turrboo.com/channel/google-my-business) updates that appear in local search

### **Where organic wins**

**It builds trust.** People follow brands for useful, entertaining, or honest content. A post that teaches something earns more goodwill than an ad selling the same idea.

**It is a cheap testing lab.** Every organic post is an experiment that costs no ad money. You learn which hooks, formats, and topics your audience responds to.

**It keeps working after you stop.** A YouTube tutorial or a pin built with [Pinterest SEO](https://turrboo.com/blog/pinterest-seo-guide) in mind can surface in search for months. Paid reach ends the day the budget does.

**It doubles as customer care.** Fast replies to comments and DMs turn questions into sales and complaints into saved accounts.

### **Where organic falls short**

**Reach is limited.** Platforms show each post to a fraction of your followers. The algorithm decides who sees it, not you.

**Growth is slow.** A new account can post for months before reach picks up. Teams chasing a quarterly target often lose patience here.

**The cost is hidden in hours.** Organic is free in ad spend only. Planning, creating, posting, and replying across several platforms takes real staff time.

Batching posts in advance with a [scheduling and publishing tool](https://turrboo.com/features/publishing) is where most teams recover those hours.

### **Organic metrics to track**

*   **Reach and impressions:** how many people saw the post
*   **Engagement rate:** interactions divided by reach
*   **Saves and shares:** the strongest signals that content has value
*   **Follower growth:** net new followers over a set period
*   **Link clicks:** tracked with UTM parameters so you can see site visits
*   **Response time:** how fast you answer comments and DMs

![Image 1: Organic vs Paid Social Media](https://turrboo.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Fvw2ug24x%2Fproduction%2F109d8d5b9a25d0e4c894c4e057cc60391dab584d-1000x667.jpg%3Fw%3D700%26q%3D80&w=3840&q=75)

Paid social is any content a platform shows because you paid it to. You set the budget, audience, and goal inside each platform's ads manager, such as [Meta Ads Manager](https://www.facebook.com/business/tools/ads-manager) for Facebook and Instagram.

*   Boosted posts: an existing organic post promoted to a wider audience
*   Feed, Stories, and Reels ads built in an ads manager
*   Lead generation ads with in-platform forms
*   Retargeting ads shown to past site visitors or video viewers
*   Paid creator partnerships, labeled as sponsored

Platforms charge in a few ways. Cost per click (CPC) bills each click. Cost per mille (CPM) bills every 1,000 impressions. Many campaigns optimize for cost per result, such as a lead or a purchase.

### **Where paid wins**

**Precise targeting.** You choose location, age, interests, and behavior. Retargeting reaches people who already visited your site or watched your videos.

**Speed.** A campaign can reach thousands of people within hours of approval. That suits launches, events, and time-bound [social media campaigns](https://turrboo.com/blog/social-media-campaigns).

**Predictable scale.** Once a campaign hits a healthy cost per result, more budget usually buys more results. Organic offers no such dial.

**Direct attribution.** Ads managers report spend against clicks, leads, and sales. Finance teams can see the return line by line.

### **Where paid falls short**

**It stops when the money stops.** Paid reach does not compound. Pause the budget and visibility drops to your organic baseline.

**Costs rise with competition.** Ad prices are set by auction. Crowded categories and peak seasons push CPM and CPC up.

**Ad fatigue sets in.** The same creative shown too often loses attention. Teams need fresh ads every few weeks to hold performance.

**It needs active management.** Bids, audiences, and creatives need regular review. Someone has to own the account.

### **Paid metrics to track**

*   **Impressions and frequency:** how many people saw the ad, and how often
*   **Click-through rate (CTR):** clicks divided by impressions
*   **CPC and CPM:** what each click or 1,000 impressions cost
*   **Cost per result:** what each lead, signup, or sale cost
*   **Return on ad spend (ROAS):** revenue earned per dollar spent

Start with organic in almost every case, then add paid once you know what works. The right balance depends on your situation, not on a fixed ratio.

**You're a new brand with a small budget.** Lead with organic. Post consistently for a couple of months, ideally at the [best times to post](https://turrboo.com/blog/best-times-to-post-on-social-media) for your audience. That gives paid a proven post to amplify later.

**You have a launch, event, or sale on a deadline.** Use paid. Organic can't guarantee reach by a specific date. Keep organic running alongside so the campaign lands on an active profile.

**You have an engaged audience and steady content.** Keep organic as the core. Put paid budget behind the posts that already outperform.

**You run a local business.** Combine Google Business Profile updates, organic posts, and small location-targeted ads. Local searchers see your profile before they see your feed.

**You sell B2B.** Organic LinkedIn posts from founders and staff often earn strong trust. A clear plan for [LinkedIn for business](https://turrboo.com/blog/linkedin-for-business) pairs well with LinkedIn ads for retargeting and lead forms.

One rule holds across all five: spend on paid only what you can measure. If you can't tie a campaign to a result, cut it back until you can.

The most reliable hybrid model is simple: organic finds the winners, paid scales them, and paid results feed back into organic. Here is that loop as a weekly workflow.

1.   **Plan an organic calendar around three to five content themes.** A clear [social media content strategy](https://turrboo.com/blog/how-to-build-a-winning-social-media-content-strategy) makes results comparable. You can see whether tutorials beat behind-the-scenes posts.
2.   **Tag every link with UTM parameters.** Add source, medium, and campaign tags with a tool like Google's [Campaign URL Builder](https://ga-dev-tools.google/campaign-url-builder/). Your web analytics can then separate organic visits from paid visits.
3.   **Review organic performance every week.** Shortlist the top one or two posts. Rank them on [social media metrics](https://turrboo.com/blog/social-media-metri

results.title: 6 strategies for harnessing travel and tourism marketing
results.markdown:
Title: 6 strategies for harnessing travel and tourism marketing

URL Source: https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/travel-and-tourism-marketing

Published Time: 2022-11-25T15:52:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Travel is back, and it’s [coming back strong](https://www.entrepreneur.com/living/this-is-what-travel-will-look-like-in-a-post-pandemic-world/377253). Since 2020, [US digital ad spend](https://www.statista.com/statistics/235955/online-ad-spending-of-the-us-leisure-travel-industry/) has been steadily increasing year over year. In 2023, it’s projected that spend will reach $4.54 billion USD, a 12% increase from 2022.

For travel marketers, this growth signals that it’s time for a fresh tourism marketing strategy. To help you build a programmatic strategy for travel that drives results, we’re unpacking the latest trends in the industry, and sharing top-of-mind travel and tourism marketing strategies.

## Travel and tourism trends

It’s clear that the [travel revival](https://www.travelpulse.com/opinions/column/pandemic-travel-revival.html) has started. Across the industry, there have been positive signs, from [increasing traffic in US airports](https://www.tsa.gov/coronavirus/passenger-throughput) to [growing ad spend](https://www.statista.com/statistics/235955/online-ad-spending-of-the-us-leisure-travel-industry/). Let’s dive into some of those travel and tourism marketing trends in detail.

### Domestic tourism is booming

Although international destinations also account for a large amount of US consumer spending on travel, it’s important not to forget about domestic travellers. Americans go on over 2.29 billion domestic trips every year!

In fact, [one study](https://passport-photo.online/blog/domestic-tourism/) found that 96% of the survey respondents took (or planned to take) at least one domestic leisure trip in 2022. And, 80% of those respondents described their most recent local travel experience as positive or very positive.

### Consumers are looking to travel with purpose

Travellers are becoming increasingly value driven, which is influencing their decisions when purchasing travel products and services. [Seventy-two percent](https://www.americanexpress.com/en-us/travel/discover/get-inspired/global-travel-trends) of travellers are looking to have a positive impact and support communities and businesses through tourism.

Sixty-nine percent of consumers said they are more mindful of choosing hotels and airlines that align with their values and support diversity and inclusion within their workforce. Travellers are also becoming more [eco-friendly](https://www.americanexpress.com/en-us/travel/discover/get-inspired/global-travel-trends) and many are looking to support airline brands that are sustainable (68%) and carbon negative (55%).

### Personalized experiences are for travellers, too

Consumers are increasingly expecting [personalized marketing experiences](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/personalizing-your-digital-marketing-strategy) at every touch point through the marketing funnel, from their first exposure to a brand, all the way to their post-purchase experience.

This is relevant across all industries, including travel and tourism marketing. Personalized marketing in travel is now a must-have. [According to Skift](https://skift.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/09/Skift-Boxever-The_Future-of-Personalized-Marketing.pdf), That personalized touch can drive increased conversion rates and revenue, and improve customer loyalty.

## 6 travel and tourism marketing strategies

Here are 6 travel and tourism marketing strategies that will help map out your next travel campaign.

### 1. Use geotargeting to reach nearby consumers

[Geotargeting](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/mapping-out-your-geotargeting-strategy) is the practice of delivering content to a consumer—via mobile or web—using the geographic location information of the recipient. For travel and tourism marketing, it’s the perfect strategy for tapping into the booming domestic tourism market.

For example, if a destination marketing organization (DMO) based in Nevada wants to attract travellers from their neighbour state, California, they can leverage [geofencing](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/what-is-geofencing) to capture the attention of people located there. Geofencing targets users based on the geographic location information of the recipient. This tactic draws a virtual fence around a geographic location, so that users who enter that “fenced” area are served your ads.

You can target audiences using location data like country, state, postal or zip code, or even a specific address. If you’re looking to attract domestic consumers, geotargeting is one strategy that will help you remind travellers of what’s in their own backyard.

### 2. Use video to entice consumers to book

Travel is an emotional experience for consumers. Therefore, leveraging a channel that speaks to that emotion is a great way to capture the interest of your target audience. [Video](https://www.stackadapt.com/video-advertising) is particularly effective for travel because it’s an engaging and immersive medium that uses visual cues to create emotion in viewers.

Travel brands can use [video advertising](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/programmatic-video-advertising) to engage viewers with storytelling and showcase the experiences that they are offering. By engaging a viewer’s emotion, your video may entice them to book a weekend getaway at your hotel, or travel to your resort for the gorgeous beaches. When you run your video campaign on [connected TV](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/introduction-to-connected-tv) (CTV), you can capture and hold user attention particularly well because CTV provides a natural, full-screen experience.

Ads shown on CTV are highly viewable, and are served in an environment in which the audience is already engaged. When watching a connected TV device, viewers understand and accept that ads are part of the viewing experience.

Knowing this, they are more receptive to them. These benefits combined with CTV’s enhanced targeting options and inventory selection are just part of why we’re seeing CTV overtake linear ad spend. For travel marketers, CTV is the perfect channel for delivering video ads that will entice consumers to book travel.

### 3. Appeal to the audiences through eye-catching creative

Video is a fantastic channel for emotionally engaging consumers, but all formats of ad creative have a similar effect. Your campaign’s messaging, regardless of the medium, plays an important role in capturing the interest of your target audience. Build creatives that resonate with your target audience, so you can attract the travellers who are most likely to engage with your campaign.

When running a travel campaign, use your ads to grab the interest of your audience by showing content that is relevant to them. For example, target users in cold geographic regions with images that show warm and sunny destinations. Hook your target demographic in the first few seconds by using language that speaks to them, intrigues them, or spurs an emotional response.

### 4. Leverage contextual advertising to reach the right audience

[Contextual targeting](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/behavioural-vs-contextual) in travel and tourism marketing can enable you to reach audiences who are ready to travel. This targeting tactic uses algorithms to place ads based on keywords, website content, and other metadata. This way, users are targeted based on the environment in which an ad appears, which places focus on the consumer’s current frame of mind to show an ad that is hyper relevant.

Capturing an audience that is currently receptive to travel is the key to success. For example, by using contextual advertising to target content like, “best destinations in 2023,” you can reach travellers who are planning to travel soon, or planning to travel in the near future. To reach the people who are considering travel, make sure to first engage with those who are most interested—they will be more likely to book a trip.

### 5. Measure travel advertising results with a brand lift study

[Brand lift studies](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/brand-lift-studies) go beyond traditional metrics, like impressions, to help you measure a travel campaign’s impact on [consumer perceptions and behaviour](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/how-agencies-thrive-podcast-episode-11/). A brand lift study measures the impact of your campaigns across all your programmatic channels, typically providing a picture of the consumer sentiment and brand affinity of people who have been exposed to your media.

For travel marketing, it can be used to measure the impact of upper funnel campaigns on your consumers’ perception of your brand. Or, leverage it to measure consideration or purchase intent in the mid- to lower funnel.

results.markdown:
Title: How to Use Google My Business for Your Coffee Shop: A Step-by-Step Guide

URL Source: https://www.tryperdiem.com/blog/google-business-profile-coffee-shop-guide

Published Time: 2025-06-19T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
## **TLDR**

When people search for “coffee near me” or “best cappuccino in town,” Google is often their first stop. For coffee shops, this is both a challenge and a huge opportunity. If your business doesn’t appear in local search results, you’re invisible to a large chunk of potential customers. On the other hand, when you set up your Google Business Profile correctly, you can attract foot traffic, grow app orders, and gain loyal local fans—without spending money on ads.

That’s where Google My Business comes in. It’s free, powerful, and made for small businesses to stand out in their neighborhoods. As one [business owner of Ram Asrey Sweets](https://business.google.com/in/business-profile/) puts it,

> _“Our top priority was to spread our visibility to the new people that are coming in to the city. We did this with Google Business Profile.”_

In this guide, we’ll walk through how coffee shop owners like you can set up and optimize your Google Business Profile from scratch. You’ll also see how some cafés have used it to get thousands of app downloads and grow faster. Let’s get started.

![Image 1: __wf_reserved_inherit](https://cdn.per-diem.co/tryperdiem-assets/cms/blog-posts/google-business-profile-coffee-shop-guide/6853e997ad6c386c1059e467_Untitled-20design-20-2-.png)

## **What is Google My Business (Now Google Business Profile)?**

[Google Business Profile](https://www.google.com/intl/en_pk/business/) is a free tool that lets you manage how your coffee shop appears across Google Search and Maps. It lets you control your store information, hours, photos, customer reviews, and more—all from one place. It’s what powers that small box you often see when you search for a local business.

Over the past few years, Google has made this tool even easier to use. You can now manage most of it directly from a regular Google search or the Maps app, without logging into a separate dashboard. This update makes it simple to post updates, respond to reviews, and make quick edits to your listing on the go.

Most importantly, it’s completely free, and that’s rare for something so useful in digital marketing.

‍

## **Why Google Business Profile is Crucial for Coffee Shops**

Coffee is local. Unlike online stores or subscription services, your business relies on people walking in, sitting down, or grabbing their daily cup on the way to work. That’s why local visibility matters so much.

Google Business Profile helps by placing your coffee shop on the map—literally. When someone searches for coffee in your area, your profile can show up in the top search results, along with directions, photos, and reviews. This “local 3-pack” is prime digital real estate, and claiming your profile is the first step to getting there.

Having a well-maintained Google listing also builds trust. Reviews, updated photos, and correct hours show customers that your business is active and reliable. With most searches now happening on mobile, especially for food and drink, it’s one of the most effective tools to get noticed by people already nearby.

According to [search endurance](https://searchendurance.com/google-business-profile-statistics/), 90% of weekday business calls originate from Google Business Profiles, highlighting its role as a primary channel for customer contact. That means if your profile is missing or incomplete, you could be missing out on real orders and conversations with people who are ready to visit.

‍

## **Step-by-Step Guide to Setting Up Your Profile**

Let’s break down exactly how to set up your coffee shop on Google the right way. These steps are beginner-friendly but powerful enough to help you stand out.

#### Step 1: Create or Claim Your Business

Start by going to the Google Business Profile site. Sign in with your Google account and search for your coffee shop. If it already exists, you can claim it. If not, you can create a new listing from scratch.

Fill in your business name and category. Choose “Coffee shop” or a related term, rather than something too broad like “Restaurant.” This will help you show up in the most relevant searches.

#### Step 2: Enter Basic Info

Next, fill out your address, phone number, business hours, and website. Make sure all this information is accurate and matches what’s listed on your other platforms, like [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/tryperdiem) or your website.

Inconsistent details across the internet can confuse both Google and customers. That’s why it’s good practice to double-check everything before publishing.

#### Step 3: Verify Your Business

Google will ask you to verify your coffee shop before your listing goes live. This usually involves receiving a postcard with a code to your business address, though some businesses get the option to verify via phone or email.

Verification is essential. It confirms to Google (and customers) that your business is real, operating, and trustworthy.

#### Step 4: Add High-Quality Photos

Once your business is verified, start uploading great photos. Don’t just stop at the storefront—show off your lattes, your seating area, the barista counter, and the mood of your space.

People often choose where to get coffee based on how the place feels. Clear, warm photos help you communicate that vibe. Regularly updated images also signal that your business is active and well-loved.

#### Step 5: Write an Engaging Business Description

Use this section to tell your story. Are you a cozy neighborhood café serving locally roasted beans? Do you specialize in seasonal drinks or plant-based options? This is where you can stand out.

Try to include a few keywords that describe your offerings and location. Something like “independent espresso bar in downtown Atlanta” works better than a generic line like “we love coffee.”

#### Step 6: Link to Your App Instead of a Menu

Traditionally, many coffee shops add a PDF menu or website link to their Google profile. That can work, but there’s a better option: linking to your [mobile app menu](https://www.tryperdiem.com/mobile-app/barrio-bagel-and-slice). PDF menus often go out of date, and it’s easy to forget to update them. Your app menu, on the other hand, stays current because it updates automatically with your [POS system](https://squareup.com/us/en/app-marketplace/app/per-diem). So when you change prices or add a new drink in-store, the app shows it right away. This helps customers always see the latest version of your menu without any extra work from you.

For example, [Think Coffee,](https://thinkcoffee.com/) an independent coffee brand, saw a surge in app usage after placing their app download link directly in their Google profile. They now have thousands of downloads and regular app-based orders that come in daily. Similarly, [Barrio Bagel and Slice](https://barriobagelandslice.com/) integrated their app link into their profile and noticed a sharp increase in new user sign-ups and in-app orders, all without spending extra on advertising.

This tactic turns casual searchers into loyal app users, right from the first Google interaction.

#### Step 7: Enable Messaging and Booking Features

Once your listing is live, turn on features that make it easier for customers to connect with you. Google allows users to message businesses directly through their listings. If you have a system for handling messages—like answering quick questions about hours or availability—it’s a great way to build rapport with new customers.

You can also add links to your reservation or ordering system if you offer advance orders, pre-booked coffee subscriptions, or space rentals for events. These small conveniences create a smooth experience and help convert interest into action.

## **Optimizing Your Coffee Shop's Profile**

After your profile is set up, the next step is to keep it active and optimized. This doesn’t mean a complete overhaul every week, just small, consistent updates that show customers you’re engaged.

#### Post Regular Updates

Use the “Posts” feature to share specials, events, new menu items, or seasonal drinks. Treat it like a mini social media post. A photo and a few lines are enough to keep your audience in the loop and show Google that your business is active.

#### Respond to Reviews

Whether the review is glowing or not-so-great, responding shows you care. Thank your happy customers and address concerns respectfully. This not only helps with customer retention, but it also makes a good impression on people checking your reviews before visiting.
